Machine Translation## Title

Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning for Low-Resource Machine Translation

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Neural machine translation (NMT) for low-resource language pairs suffers
from data sparsity. While massively multilingual pretrained models (e.g., mBART,
NLLB) provide a strong foundation, they are expensive to deploy and fine-tune,
and their coverage of truly low-resource languages remains uneven. Current
approaches either rely on large-scale back-translation (which introduces noise)
or on pivoting through a high-resource language (which compounds errors). There
is no established method that efficiently selects high-quality synthetic
training data from monolingual corpora without requiring a seed translation
system or a large teacher model.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
Cross-lingual sentence embeddings, learned via a lightweight
contrastive objective on a small bilingual dictionary (≤5k entries), can
retrieve high-quality parallel sentence pairs from monolingual corpora to
augment a small seed parallel corpus. An NMT model fine-tuned on this augmented
data will outperform: (1) training on the seed corpus alone, (2) standard
back-translation augmentation, and (3) using generic multilingual sentence
encoders (e.g., LaBSE) for retrieval, particularly when the total compute budget
is ≤1 GPU-day.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Stage1: Lightweight Cross-Lingual Retriever1. Input:5,000 word-level
translation pairs from a bilingual dictionary (or automatically induced via
unsupervised bilingual lexicon induction). Two large monolingual corpora (source
side: ~5M sentences, target side: ~5M sentences).

2 Encoder: A small dual-encoder Transformer (2 layers,256-dim hidden,4 heads —
≈6M parameters) initialized independently on source and target monolingual
data via masked language modeling (1 epoch each).
3 Contrastive alignment: For each dictionary entry, sample an equal number of
unrelated source/target words as negatives. Optimize with InfoNCE loss + a
margin of0.3. No back-translation or parallel data is needed.
4 Retrieval: Encode all sentences from both monolingual corpora with the
aligned encoder. For each source sentence, retrieve the top-5 target
sentences by cosine similarity. Apply a confidence threshold (≥0.7) to retain
only high-confidence pairs.

Stage2: NMT Fine-Tuning1. Seed parallel corpus:20k sentence pairs.

2 Augmented corpus: Seed + high-confidence retrieved pairs (expected
yield:50k–150k depending on language pair — accept50k as minimum).
3 Model:6-layer Transformer (512-dim,8-head encoder-decoder) — intentionally
kept small.
4 Training: Standard label-smoothed cross-entropy (label smoothing ε=0.1), Adam
(β₁=0.9, β₂=0.98), inverse sqrt learning rate scheduler (warmup4000 steps).
Batch size4096 tokens. Early stopping based on dev perplexity (patience5).1
GPU-day budget on a single A100.

Dataset / Benchmark| Split | Size | Source |

|---|---|---| | Bilingual dictionary |5,000 pairs | Wiktionary / PanLex /
automatic induction | | Seed parallel (train) |20k pairs | JW300 or Tatoeba | |
Monolingual (source) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | |
Monolingual (target) |5M sentences | CommonCrawl / Leipzig Corpora | | Dev |2k
pairs | FLORES-200 dev split | | Test |2k pairs | FLORES-200 devtest split |

Language pair: Gujarati → English (gu-en), a genuinely low-resource pair with
under100k publicly available parallel sentences. The same pipeline should also
be evaluated on a second pair (e.g., Kazakh → English) to ensure results are not
language-specific.

nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp) — primary metric- chrF++
(character-level) — secondary, captures morphologically faithful translations-
COMET (wmt22-comet-da) — neural metric for semantic adequacy- Retrieval
precision@1 on held-out bilingual dictionary entries (to validate the retriever
quality in Stage1)

• Effective augmentation yield: number of retrieved pairs above the confidence
thresholdAll NMT models are run with 3 random seeds. We report means with95%
bootstrap confidence intervals.

Baselines| # | Method | Key Difference from CREST-MT |

|---|---|---| | B1 | Seed-only fine-tuning | No data augmentation | | B2 | Seed
+ standard back-translation | Uses a target→source model to back-translate
target monolingual data | | B3 | Seed + LaBSE-based retrieval (Feng et al.,2022)
| Replaces our contrastive retriever with the publicly available LaBSE encoder |
| B4 | mBART-50 fine-tuned on seed (4 layers unfrozen) | Multilingual pretrained

persist in larger models.

Expected Failure Modes| Failure Mode | Likelihood | Mitigation |

depends on how well dictionary covers the monolingual data | Fall back to a

quartiles; if low-confidence pairs actively hurt, use confidence-weighted
training loss | | Dictionary quality is poor (many incorrect entries) | Low for
Wiktionary; Medium for automatically induced dictionaries | B6 ablation tests

Research Proposal: Self-Specification Alignment for LLM-Generated Code##
Title
Self-Specification Alignment: Closing the Validation Loop for LLM Code
Generation Using Automatically Generated Behavioral Oracles

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
LLM-based code generation is evaluated almost entirely on observed test
coverage — does the generated code pass the few unit tests that ship with the
benchmark (HumanEval, MBPP, etc.)? This creates a well-known gap: code can pass
the provided tests while being functionally incorrect on edge cases or failing
to align with the full natural-language specification. In real software
engineering, the gap between "passes tests" and "correct" is where bugs live.

Current approaches (pass@k, test-time repair) attempt to close this gap by
sampling many candidates or brute-force re-prompting on test failure, but they
never broaden the test oracle itself. The specification is only consulted by the
human providing the original tests — the LLM never generates a specification it
then holds itself accountable to.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis> H1: For a given programming problem described in natural language,
an LLM can generate a behavioral oracle (a set of property-based or
example-based tests) that is more complete than the small set of tests provided
in the benchmark, and that oracle can be used to detect and repair incorrect
solutions that pass the original tests.

▌ H2: This self-specification + self-repair loop improves functional
▌ correctness over the baseline pass@k on the original test set, with
▌ diminishing returns bounded by the quality of the LLM-generated oracle.

The key claim is that the marginal correctness signal of self-generated tests —
tests the model writes about its own spec — is positive relative to the original
test set, even though the model generates both the code and the tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
The proposal consists of three stages:

Stage1 — Conditional Test GenerationGiven a problem description (docstring +
signature + examples), prompt the LLM to generate k additional test cases that:

• Cover edge cases (empty input, boundary values, large inputs, type
mismatches)
• Exercise postconditions stated in the docstring- Include both positive
(should pass) and negative (should reject/invalid input) casesConstraints:
the generated tests must be executable and self-contained.

Stage2 — Self-Specification ValidationFor each candidate solution:

1 Run it against the original benchmark tests. If it fails → discard.
2 Run it against the self-generated tests from Stage1. If it fails → flag for
repair.
3 Metric: oracle disagreement rate — what fraction of candidates that pass
original tests are caught by self-generated tests?

Stage3 — Iterative Self-RepairFor every candidate that passes original tests but
fails self-generated tests:

• Return the failing test(s) + failure message to the LLM as a repair prompt.
• Generate a repaired candidate.
• Re-validate against both original and self-generated tests.
• Repeat up to N iterations (or until all tests pass).
• Measure: success rate of repair (fraction of flagged candidates that pass all
tests after repair), and added correctness (fraction of originally-passed
problems that are now correct on a held-out test set).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark| Benchmark | Language | Problems | Relevance |

|---|---|---|---| | HumanEval+ (Liu et al.,2023) | Python |164 | Extended tests
beyond original HumanEval; serves as ground-truth oracle | | MBPP+ (Liu et
al.,2023) | Python |399 | Another standard; extended tests | | CodeContests
(DeepMind,2022) | Python/C++ | ~10k | Harder problems with rich test suites |

Use HumanEval+/MBPP+ as primary (known ground-truth oracles). The original test
set (5–10 tests) serves as the "provided tests"; the extended tests (Liu et
al.'s hand-audited additions or self-generated) serve as the evaluation oracle.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Definition |

|---|---| | pass@k | Fraction of problems solved by any of k samples using
original tests | | self-gap | Fraction of pass@k solutions that fail
self-generated tests (oracle disagreement) | | repair recovery | Fraction of
self-gap failures that are repaired to pass all tests | | added-correctness@k |
Fraction of problems that only become correct after self-specification + repair
(true positives) | | over-repair rate | Fraction of problems where self-repair
breaks a previously correct solution (regression) | | test oracle precision |
Fraction of self-generated test failures that correspond to actual errors (on
held-out ground truth) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. pass@k greedy — standard top-1 sampling, no repair.

2 pass@k sample — standard sampling (k=10,100,200).
3 self-repair (original tests only) — repair using only the original benchmark
tests (to isolate the value of additional self-generated tests).
4 LLM-as-judge (no execution) — ask the LLM whether the solution is correct,
without running tests; report as a soft ablation of the execution signal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Ablations| Ablation | Question Answered |

|---|---| | No self-generated tests | Is the self-specification oracle adding
signal beyond just re-prompting? | | Self-generated tests from a different model
| Is the quality of self-generated tests model-dependent? (e.g., GPT-4o
generates tests, DeepSeek generates code) | | Single repair vs. multi-turn
repair | Does repair degrade after1–2 iterations (overfitting to generated
tests)? | | Docstring-only vs. docstring + signature + example | How much
specification context is needed to generate useful tests? | | Temperature
ablation on test generation | Does diverse test generation (high T) improve
oracle coverage? |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Expected Failure Modes1. Circular validation — The LLM generates tests that
match its code bugs instead of the spec. If both code and tests share the same
blind spot, the oracle adds no signal → large self-gap is actually large
false-negative rate. Mitigation: measure precision on human-audited extended
tests (HumanEval+).

2 Over-repair / regressions — Repairing against self-generated tests breaks
correctness on the original tests or introduces new bugs. Mitigation: always
check original tests post-repair; report over-repair rate explicitly.
3 Specification underspecification — The docstring itself is ambiguous or
underspecified, so no amount of test generation can disambiguate it. The
method is bounded by the quality of the input specification. Mitigation:
filter problems where human annotators deem the spec unambiguous and report
results conditioned on specification clarity.
4 Test generation cost — Generating k test cases per problem × n samples ×
repair iterations is significantly more expensive than sampling alone.
Mitigation: report token cost per solved problem; treat this as a proposed
quality-cost tradeoff.
5 Model self-attribution bias — The model may be overly agreeable with its own
generated tests, failing to challenge its code against rigorous oracles. The
cross-model ablation (tests from model A, code from model B) tests this
directly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Proposed Experimental Protocol1. For each problem, generate self-specification
tests (k=20) from the docstring.

2 Draw100 code samples per problem (pass@k evaluation).
3 For each sample passing original tests: run self-generated tests; flag
failures.
4 Attempt repair (up to3 iterations) on each flagged candidate.
5 Evaluate final correctness against HumanEval+ extended tests (ground truth).
6 Report: pass@k (baseline), added-correctness (method), self-gap, repair
recovery, over-repair rate, token cost per problem.

well-documented accuracy issues:

to0.7 on factual QA).

follow multi-criteria instructions consistently, collapsing dimensions or
ignoring criteria.

— scores that are calibrated, debiased, and accompanied by uncertainty — rather
than simply fast scores.

judgments from multiple diverse evaluator LLMs with explicit uncertainty
estimation, and calibrating the resulting scores against a small human-annotated

holistic-judgment baseline, while also reducing known biases (position,
verbosity) and providing well-calibrated uncertainty estimates.

2  Correctness            Are factual claims accurate? (for knowledge tasks)

consistent?

constraints?

criterion-specific prompt that includes the rubric definition, the prompt, and

Research Proposal: Multi-Agent LLM Systems for Clinical Trial Eligibility
Screening## Title
TrialMatch: A Structured Multi-Agent Debate Framework for
Zero-Shot Clinical Trial Eligibility Screening

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Problem
Clinical trial enrollment is the bottleneck of medical research.
Eligibility screening — determining whether a patient's unstructured EHR notes
satisfy a trial's inclusion/exclusion criteria — is currently performed manually
by coordinators. This is slow, error-prone, and does not scale to the ~400,000
trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Single-pass LLM prompting achieves ~70–75% F1 on eligibility classification
(TrialGPT,2024), but suffers from two issues: (a) it hallucinates criterion
matches for ambiguous or missing data, and (b) it does not handle contradictory
criteria across multiple trials for the same patient.

Open question: Can a multi-agent debate architecture, where specialized agents
argue for and against each criterion, outperform a single monolithic LLM on this
task?

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Hypothesis
A multi-agent debate system — where one agent argues for criterion
satisfaction (citing specific evidence), a second argues against, and a judge
agent synthesizes the final decision — will improve F1 by ≥5 points over a
single-pass LLM with equal total inference cost, because forced adversarial
reasoning reduces hallucination on borderline criteria.

Null hypothesis: Multi-agent debate does not significantly outperform
single-pass prompting when both use the same backbone LLM and comparable token
budgets.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Method
### Architecture: TrialMatchThe system operates in three stages per
patient-trial pair:

1 Evidence Extraction: An extractor agent reads the patient note + trial
criteria and produces a structured table mapping each criterion to the spans
of text that are relevant (or marks the criterion as "no evidence in note").
2 Adversarial Debate (per criterion):

• Pro Agent — given the criterion and extracted evidence, argues why the
patient meets this criterion.
• Con Agent — given the same evidence, argues why the patient does not meet it.
• Each agent is temperature-decayed (T=0.7 →0.3) over3 rounds; they see each
other's arguments.

3 Aggregation & Prediction:

• Judge Agent — reads the debate transcripts for all criteria and produces:
• A binary eligibility decision (eligible / ineligible)
• A confidence score - Citations to specific spans in the original
noteBackbone: Llama-3.1-70B (or a similarly capable open model), quantized to
allow multi-agent rollouts on a single A100.

Prompt structure: Each agent is prompted with a role persona (e.g., "You are a
conservative clinical reviewer who requires explicit documentation before
approving") to ensure separation of perspectives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dataset / Benchmark
Primary: TrialGPT benchmark (Jin et al.,2024) —183 patient
summaries (from TREC Clinical Trials) and3,500+ trial-criterion pairs with
expert-annotated eligibility labels. This is the standard zero-shot benchmark.

Secondary (robustness): N2C22018 (Adverse Drug Events cohort) — convert the ADE
extraction task into criterion-style screening for a drug trial; measure
cross-dataset transfer.

Validation method:5-fold patient-level cross-validation on TrialGPT. No patient
appears in both train and test folds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Evaluation Metrics| Metric | Rationale |

|---|---| | Macro F1 (primary) | Balanced measure for binary eligibility;
primary metric in TrialGPT | | Criterion-level accuracy | Per-criterion match vs
annotator labels (from TrialGPT's fine-grained labels) | | Precision vs Recall
tradeoff | Important for clinical use — false positives (enrolling an ineligible
patient) are costlier than false negatives | | Mean confidence calibration (ECE)
| Judge confidence should correlate with correctness | | Debate round
convergence | Does additional debate rounds (>3) change the final decision?
(sensitivity analysis) | | Token cost | Total tokens consumed per patient-trial
pair (runtime cost matters for deployment) |

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Baselines1. Single-pass LLM (same backbone, same evidence extraction step, no

Clinical trial enrollment is the bottleneck of medical research.

satisfy a trial's inclusion/exclusion criteria — is currently performed manually

trials on ClinicalTrials.gov.

(TrialGPT,2024), but suffers from two issues: (a) it hallucinates criterion
matches for ambiguous or missing data, and (b) it does not handle contradictory
criteria across multiple trials for the same patient.

patient meets this criterion.

other's arguments.

Title: Structured Critical Literature Review Generation via Hierarchical
Contradiction-Aware Synthesis---

Problem
Current automated literature review systems (LLM-based or
retrieval-augmented) produce fluent but shallow summaries — they list findings
paper-by-paper, avoid conflicting results, and fail to organize knowledge into
the canonical sub-topics, debates, and open questions a human reviewer would
surface. No existing system explicitly models contradictions across papers or
generates a structured review with sections like "consensus findings,"
"conflicting evidence," and "methodological gaps."

Hypothesis
A hierarchical, contradiction-aware pipeline that (1) retrieves and
clusters papers by sub-topic, (2) extracts claim-level triples (method, finding,
direction of effect), and (3) explicitly identifies and resolves or flags
contradictions, will produce literature reviews that are rated by domain experts
as more organized, more critical, and more useful than retrieval-augmented
baselines that only summarize per-paper or per-topic.

Method
Stage1 — Hierarchical topic structuring. Given a query (e.g.
"chain-of-thought reasoning"), query a paper corpus (e.g. S2ORC / Semantic
Scholar) and cluster retrieved abstracts using a hierarchical embedding +
LLM-labeling pipeline (HDBSCAN on SBERT embeddings, then GPT-4o-mini assigns
canonical section headings).

Stage2 — Claim extraction and contradiction detection. For each paper, extract
structured claim triples (entity, predicate, direction/sign) via a fine-tuned
DeBERTa-v3 or prompted LLM. Within each sub-topic cluster, compare claim triples
for directional mismatches (e.g. "CoT improves accuracy on GSM8K" vs "CoT does
not improve accuracy on GSM8K"). Flag contradictions with supporting citations
on both sides.

Stage3 — Contradiction-aware synthesis. Generate the review section-by-section
using a controlled generation loop: (a) draft a section from the consensus
claims, (b) conditionally append a "conflicting evidence" sub-section if
contradictions were detected, (c) append an "open questions" sub-section
identifying gaps where evidence is absent or contradictory.

Stage4 — Citation grounding and fact verification. Each generated claim is
back-linked to the original source passage. A lightweight fact-verification step
(NLI-based, e.g. TrueTeacher) verifies whether the generated claim is entailed
by the cited passage. Unverifiable claims are removed or softened.

Dataset / Benchmark- Corpus: Semantic Scholar Open Research Corpus (S2ORC) — ~8M
papers, with full text when available. Restrict to4-5 well-surveyed domains
(e.g., LLM reasoning, protein folding, adversarial robustness, representation
learning, NLP for low-resource languages).

• Gold-standard reviews: For each domain, collect2-3 human-written survey
papers (e.g. from arXiv, JMLR, ACL anthology). Segment into sections as
ground-truth structure.
• Review quality evaluation set: Construct50 query-review pairs per domain,
each with3 expert ratings along organization, coverage, critical depth, and
usefulness (1–5 Likert).

Evaluation Metrics| Dimension | Metric | How measured |

|---|---|---| | Structure | Section overlap (ROUGE-L / Jaccard on section
headings) | Against human survey TOC | | Coverage | Recall of cited papers from
human survey reference list | Macro-averaged per section | | Critical depth |
Contradiction recall — fraction of known conflicting findings surfaced |
Hand-labeled conflict set | | Faithfulness | % of claims entailed by cited
passages | NLI-based verification + human spot-check | | Overall quality |
Expert rating (1–5) on organization, usefulness | Blind rating by3 domain
experts |

Baselines1. Naive RAG — Retrieve top-20 papers, concatenate abstracts, prompt
GPT-4o to write a review.

2 Per-paper summarization — Summarize each paper individually, then concatenate
under LLM-generated headings (Liu et al.,2024-style).
3 Topic-cluster summarization — Cluster papers by topic, summarize cluster,
then synthesize (similar to Scim,2024).
4 Ours w/o contradiction detection — Same pipeline but skip Stage2
contradiction flagging (ablate the core mechanism).

Ablations- A1: Remove hierarchical clustering → flat topic list (tests whether
hierarchy improves organization).

• A2: Remove fact-verification filter (tests whether filtering reduces
hallucination at the cost of coverage).
• A3: Replace GPT-4o claim extraction with fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 (tests whether
a smaller model suffices).
• A4: Remove contradiction-aware sub-section generation → always write
consensus-only text (tests the value of explicit contradiction flagging vs.
implicit handling).

Expected Failure Modes1. Contradictions are rare or subtle. Most papers in a
well-matured field may agree on fundamentals, leaving little for the
contradiction module to surface. Mitigation: evaluate on at least one rapidly
evolving domain (e.g., LLM reasoning post-2023) where disagreements are common.

2 Claim extraction noise propagates. A false-positive contradiction (two claims
that appear contradictory but differ in experimental setup) degrades the
review. Mitigation: require supporting citations on both sides; add a
confidence threshold for contradiction flagging.
3 Expert raters prefer concise over critical. Human readers may rate a fluent,
uncontroversial summary higher than one that honestly reports messy
disagreements. Mitigation: structure expert evaluation to score critical
depth and usefulness separately from fluency and organization.
4 Structure diversity across human surveys. Two human surveys on the same topic
often use different section taxonomies, making section-overlap metrics noisy.
Mitigation: use macro-averaged ROUGE-L and report variance; also report
expert agreement (Fleiss' κ) on organization.
5 Domain shift. A pipeline tuned on NLP papers may fail for biomedical or
physics literature where citation practices and claim phrasing differ.
Mitigation: hold out one domain for final evaluation only, to measure
generalization.
